constructivism: Learning rebuilds an internal model instead of copying facts into the head. Someone can say the right rule and still feel heavy objects fall faster.
You construct knowledge as a personal mental model, not a file transfer. Reciting a physics fact does not mean the old gut model is gone.
Knowledge is something you rebuild inside, not download. The heavy-ball intuition can survive even after you know the textbook answer.
Teaching is not pouring information in; the learner rebuilds a mental model. Knowing the fact and feeling the wrong prediction can both be true.
assimilation: Squeeze the new event into the model you already have. Label the mismatch a fluke so nothing has to change.
Keep the old picture and force the new data to fit it. Calling the demo a trick is assimilation protecting the old model.
New experience gets bent to match prior structure. You avoid updating the model by treating the conflict as a special case.
Fit incoming evidence into existing schemas. If it contradicts, explain it away instead of revising the schema.
accommodation: Rewrite the mental model so it matches what just happened. Equal fall times for heavy and light balls force that rewrite.
Change your internal picture when experience will not fit. Seeing both balls land together makes the old model untenable.
Update the schema itself, not just the story about the demo. The drop experiment is the push that requires the change.
Accommodation means the model moves. After a clear counterexample, the old prediction cannot stay.
disequilibrium: That uncomfortable mismatch between expectation and result is what drives learning. A wrong drawing that you can see is enough to create it.
Productive confusion: reality refuses your model. The error on the page is the signal, not a lecture about the error.
When prediction and outcome collide, disequilibrium begins. Visible failure of your own output makes the collision hard to ignore.
Learning starts when the model fails in front of you. A botched result can force the rethink without anyone explaining it.
mko: Someone or something that can currently do the part you cannot. Hinting software counts the same as a tutor.
More knowledgeable other: a person or tool ahead of you on the task. A peer who can do the next step qualifies.
Support can be human or designed into the tool. The MKO is whatever can perform what you still cannot.
You learn beside a more capable other — teacher, peer, or interactive help. The tool that gives the next hint is an MKO too.
zpd: The sweet spot between solo success and impossible even with help. Temporary scaffolds belong there and should fade.
ZPD is work you can finish with support but not alone. Help should thin out: full guide, then cue, then none.
Teach in the zone where guidance unlocks performance. Scaffolding is that help, and removal is part of the design.
Alone you cannot yet; with help you can. That gap is the ZPD, and worksheets that never go away are not true scaffolds.
kirschner-2006: Constructive learning does not justify unguided teaching for novices. Experts can explore more freely; beginners need structure.
They argued against minimizing guidance just because learning is constructive. Novices overload without help.
Guidance should be strong early. Open discovery works better once prior knowledge can guide the learner.
Minimal guidance fails beginners even if knowledge is constructed. Fade support as expertise grows.
constructionism: Understand by making a shareable thing in the world. A game or world others can open makes thinking public.
Learning through building an external artifact. Public make drives understanding more than private rehearsal alone.
Papert: build something real others can see or use. The artifact externalizes thought so gaps show up.
Constructionism is learn-by-making that leaves a public product. Shared worlds and projects are the classic case.
constructivism-vs-constructionism: One rebuilds a model in the head; the other learns by making something outside the head. Inside rebuild versus public make.
Constructivism is internal model change; constructionism is learning through an external artifact. Related, not the same word.
Mental-model construction versus shareable-artifact construction. Same family; different place the building happens.
Do not mix them: constructivism = inside; constructionism = outside make that drives the inside.
instructionism: Fix learning mainly by fixing how teachers explain. Better lecture delivery is treated as the whole solution.
The theory that better telling produces better learning. Improve how teachers explain, full stop.
Instructionism bets on refining teaching talk. Materials for making take a back seat to clearer lectures.
If learning is weak, improve the explanation. That is instructionism's core move.
wide-walls: Many kinds of personally meaningful projects, not merely many ages or devices. One tool, many project types.
Wide walls means variety of project genres. Story versus game on the same platform is the idea.
Support diverse project kinds learners care about. It is not about supporting every age band as the definition.
Personally meaningful variety of makes. Same environment; different project shapes.
low-floor-high-ceiling: Beginners can start easily; experts can still go deep. Same tool hosts first drag-and-drop and later complex work.
Easy entry plus room to grow. A simple first project and an advanced later project on one system.
Low floor: quick start. High ceiling: depth later. Both on the same learning tool.
Do not force a hard start or a shallow end. The tool should welcome novices and still challenge experts.
four-ps: Projects, Passion, Peers, Play. Make things you care about, with others, in a playful way.
Resnick's Four P's name creative learning: project work, personal interest, social peers, and play.
Learning design around Projects, Passion, Peers, and Play. Kindergarten creative habits for every age.
The Four P's are the creative-learning checklist: make, care, collaborate, play.
body-syntonic: Understand code by acting the motion with your body. Walk the path, then write steps that match the walk.
Pretend you are the object moving. Body first, symbols second.
Figure the program out by enacting it. Your steps become the algorithm.
Body-syntonic means the body's motion is the model for the machine's motion. Walk it, then code it.
lecture: Etymology: from Latin for reading. Historically a teacher reading material aloud.
The word lecture literally points to reading. Old form: read the text to the class.
Lecture comes from to read. The name remembers teachers reading aloud.
Not a modern invention of slides — the root is reading aloud to students.
di-vs-discovery: Not a pure either-or. Guidance should track expertise: tight for beginners, looser later.
False dichotomy between direct instruction and discovery. Expertise is the real dial.
Guide closely early; release as skill grows. Discovery versus telling is the wrong fight.
How expert the learner is decides how much guidance to give. That beats picking a camp.
faultless-communication: If they did not learn it, the instruction failed. Treat confusion as a materials problem first.
Engelmann: blame unclear teaching before blaming the student. Instruction should be faultless.
Learner error implies instructional flaw. Fix the examples and wording, not only the learner.
If the student has not learned, the teacher has not taught. That is the faultless-communication stance.
di-vs-di: lowercase di = teacher-led teaching in general; DI = Engelmann and Becker's scripted program. Same letters, different scopes.
Do not confuse everyday direct instruction with capital-D Direct Instruction. One is a style; one is a named package.
di means guided teaching broadly. DI means that specific scripted curriculum line.
Quiz trap: di versus DI. General teacher-led practice versus the Engelmann/Becker program.
gradual-release: I do, we do, you do. Teacher models, then co-solves, then students work alone.
Responsibility shifts from teacher to learner across three phases. Show, share, release.
Fully worked example first, guided practice next, independent work last. That is gradual release.
Pearson and Gallagher: move from demonstration to joint work to solo performance.
operant: Voluntary acts are shaped by what follows them. Reinforce closer approximations until the full act appears.
Consequences train chosen behaviors. Shaping rewards steps toward the target action.
Operant conditioning: after the behavior comes the consequence that makes it more or less likely.
Unlike reflexes, these are voluntary moves steered by outcomes. Reward successive approximations.
classical: Pair stimuli until an automatic response transfers. Bell with food until the bell alone triggers drool.
Involuntary response learning by association. Tests can become stress cues the same way.
Neutral signal plus unconditioned stimulus yields a conditioned response. Pavlov's bell is the template.
Classical conditioning moves automatic reactions, not voluntary choices. Pairing does the work.
positive-reinforcement: Add something liked; the behavior rises. Praise or food after the desired act.
Present a pleasant consequence to increase a behavior. That is positive reinforcement.
Behavior up because you added a wanted thing. Praise after the right move.
Plus a liked stimulus, behavior becomes more likely. Not the same as punishment.
negative-reinforcement: Remove something disliked; the behavior rises. Time-limit off after chores increases chore-doing. Not punishment.
Escape or remove an aversive thing to strengthen a behavior. Chores done then restriction lifted.
Behavior goes up because something annoying ends. Negative means remove, not bad.
Take away a disliked condition after the act; the act becomes more likely. Still reinforcement.
positive-punishment: Add something disliked; the behavior falls. Extra chores after the unwanted act.
Present an aversive consequence to decrease behavior. That is positive punishment.
Behavior down because you added something unwanted. Add work as the consequence.
Plus a disliked stimulus, behavior becomes less likely. Ask down first, then add.
negative-punishment: Remove something liked; the behavior falls. Dessert gone when dinner is unfinished.
Take away a pleasant thing to decrease a behavior. That is negative punishment.
Behavior down because a wanted thing disappears. Loss of privilege after the act.
Minus a liked stimulus, behavior becomes less likely. Remove dessert, not add chores.
reinforcement-vs-punishment: Reinforcement aims to increase behavior; punishment aims to decrease it. Positive = add; negative = remove. Up/down first, then add/remove.
Decoder: did the behavior go up or down? Then did we add or take away? Negative reinforcement is still an increase.
Increase versus decrease is the first cut. Add versus remove is the second. Do not read negative as punishment.
Four cells: +R, -R, +P, -P. Reinforcement raises rate; punishment lowers it.
cognitivism-displaced-behaviorism: Behaviorism stalled on abstract ideas, transfer, and novel problems. Watching only outward acts left the mind unexplained.
Cognitivism rose because stimulus-response could not explain flexible thought. Internal representation became necessary.
Limits of behaviorism: weak on abstraction, transfer, and new problem solving. That opened the door to cognitivism.
If only behavior is allowed as data, deep learning stays invisible. Cognitivism addressed that gap.
immediate-reinforcement: The consequence must arrive right after the behavior. Instant right/wrong beats feedback a week later.
Tight timing ties the outcome to the act. Delayed grades break that pairing.
Immediate feedback is the educational form of immediate reinforcement. Step, then signal, quickly.
Delay weakens learning from consequences. Put the result next to the move that caused it.
ecological-cognition: Study thinking in messy everyday settings, not only clean labs. Real-world memory and perception matter.
Neisser's ecological turn: cognition where people actually live. Lab-only tasks are incomplete.
How people remember and see in daily life is the object of study. Messy contexts count.
Take cognition out of the sterile experiment when you want ecological validity.
newell-simon: People build an internal problem picture and search possible moves. Not stimulus-response alone.
Problem-space search: states, operators, goals. Think through options mentally.
Internal representation plus search beats pure reaction. Newell and Simon's cognitivist move.
Solve by exploring a mental maze of states. Behaviorism's S-R story is not enough here.
cognitivist-feedback: Wrong, try again mostly nudges the next click; explaining why wrong updates the model. Fix understanding, not only the answer.
Feedback should reshape the schema. Saying only incorrect reinforces behavior without repairing the idea.
Cognitivist feedback tells why the answer failed. That is different from bare reinforcement.
Update the mental model on error. Right/wrong alone is thinner than why.
cognitive-load: Intrinsic = content hardness; extraneous = clutter; germane = useful thinking. Cut junk and sequence hard ideas.
Working memory is limited. Remove decorative load and order difficulty carefully.
Three loads: inherent difficulty, wasteful design, productive work. Design for the third by cutting the second.
Sweller: manage what competes for attention. Sequence hard material; delete useless extras.
image-principle: Instructor face on a narrated video usually does not raise learning. Little new information; can steal attention.
Mayer's Image Principle: talking-head video is often no gain. The face rarely teaches extra content.
Adding the speaker's face tends not to help outcomes. Attention may go to the face instead of the idea.
Narration plus slides can beat narration plus a non-informative face. Image Principle names that finding.
coherence-principle: Non-teaching visuals can hurt learning. Cute unrelated animations waste limited attention.
Mayer's Coherence Principle: drop seductive details that do no semantic work.
Extras that look nice but teach nothing can reduce learning. Cut them.
If a graphic does not carry the idea, it can compete with the idea. That is coherence.
self-reflection: After the work, judge how it went and why. Plan, perform, then attribute the result. Self-regulated learning.
Zimmerman: evaluate and explain causes after performance. Forethought and performance sit beside reflection.
Close the loop: what happened, and what caused it? That after-action step is self-reflection.
SRL includes looking back with a cause story, not only doing the task.
fluency-illusion: Feeling smooth after rereading is not recall ability. Familiar notes, blank quiz; practice quizzes expose it.
Ease of reading feels like knowing. It often is not. Test yourself to recalibrate.
Fluency illusion: recognition comfort masquerades as mastery. Retrieval practice breaks the illusion.
If it only feels easy while rereading, you may still fail a closed quiz. Check with a practice quiz.
monitoring-capacity: Stress can eat the attention you need to notice you are lost. After pressure drops, gaps become visible.
Metacognitive monitoring needs spare capacity. Under load, you miss your own confusion.
When stress fills working memory, self-checks fail. Later calm can reveal what you skipped.
You cannot monitor well if attention is maxed by anxiety. Capacity returns when the pressure ends.
guided-participation: Learn by watching and joining real activity beside experts. Help cook; do not only hear a talk about cooking.
Rogoff: side-by-side participation in authentic work. Sit-and-listen is one culture, not the only path.
Pitch in on the real task with more experienced people. That is guided participation.
Learning happens in joint activity, not only in lectures about the activity.
lpp: Newcomers do real low-stakes work at the edge of a community, then move inward. Simple needed tasks first.
Legitimate peripheral participation: authentic but peripheral jobs, then fuller roles.
Apprentice pattern: real contribution at the margin, growing toward the center. Not fake busywork forever.
Lave and Wenger: belong by doing real edge work in a community of practice.
cultural-variation: Allow more than one valid way to reason or represent. Do not treat one style as the only correct one.
Honor multiple reasoning styles. Translating the UI alone does not fix cultural mismatch.
Different valid representations can solve the same problem. Design should not erase that.
Cultural variation in thinking is a feature to respect, not a bug to normalize away.
zpd-vs-scaffolding: ZPD is the gap between alone and with help; scaffolding is the temporary support inside that gap. Zone versus help.
Do not confuse the zone with the props in the zone. ZPD names the gap; scaffolding names the fading help.
Zone of proximal development is not scaffolding. One is where; the other is what support you place there.
Remember: ZPD = the region; scaffolding = supports that should disappear.
mastery-oriented: Success means actually understanding, not looking better than others. I got it beats I looked smart.
Mastery goals define competence as real learning. Performance goals chase looking competent.
Goal orientation: mastery cares about skill growth more than relative ranking.
If the aim is genuine understanding, you are mastery-oriented. Showing off is a different aim.
espn-top-10: Performance-approach hunts the highlight reel; performance-avoidance dodges the blooper reel. The same dunk can become either.
Same risky play can look glorious or embarrassing. Approach wants the Top 10; avoidance fears the Not Top 10.
Approach success versus avoid failure — often on the identical attempt.
Highlight versus blooper motivation can target the same move. Mastery players may ignore both lists.
belonging: Tell students that feeling out of place is normal and temporary. That message can raise motivation and grades.
Walton and Cohen: brief belonging reassurances help, especially for marginalized students.
Normalize temporary belonging doubts. The intervention is the message, not a long course.
Social belonging can be supported by saying this feeling is common and it passes.
self-determination: Motivation needs autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Choice, can-do, and connection.
Deci and Ryan: three nutrients — autonomy, competence, relatedness.
Support meaningful choice, a sense of effectiveness, and human connection. That is SDT.
Self-determination theory names what sustains motivation beyond stickers and threats.
remote-proctoring: Systems struggled more with darker-skinned faces. Forced users get uneven harm.
Remote proctoring failed fairness on face detection for darker skin. Captive users cannot easily leave.
Uneven error rates by skin tone showed up in proctoring tools. Harm is not evenly shared.
Lesson cite: darker-skinned faces were harder for the systems. That is an ethics failure mode.
ai-feedback-demographics: Girls and underrepresented minorities got less critical feedback. Softer comments are not equal help.
Demographic skew in AI critique: some groups received gentler, less useful feedback.
Unequal critical feedback by group identity. Kindness that withholds challenge is still unequal.
If the model softens critique for some demographics, learning opportunity becomes unequal.
matthew-effect: Poorly designed tech helps students already ahead first. The gap can widen before it helps everyone.
Reich's EdTech Matthew effect: advantages accrue to the advantaged early.
Bad tool design amplifies existing privilege. Early gains go to those already resourced.
The already-advantaged gain first in learning tech when design ignores unequal starting points.
learning-styles: Matching teaching to visual/auditory/kinesthetic styles is a myth. Real differences: prior knowledge, language, access, disability.
VAK meshing failed. Design for actual learner differences, not preferred modality myths.
Learning-styles theory as meshing is not supported. Prior knowledge and access matter more.
Do not build for VAK labels. Build for knowledge gaps, language, access, and disability.
assessment: Measure this student's learning for a grade or feedback. Like reading one person's heart rate.
Assessment serves the learner being measured: score or formative comment for them.
Individual measurement for feedback or grading. Not yet a judgment of the whole program.
Assessment asks how this student is doing. Keep that separate from evaluating the tool.
evaluation: Use measures to judge whether a tool or curriculum works. Compare workout plans with the same heart-rate readings.
Evaluation judges the intervention or system, often across learners. Same meter, different use.
Program-level judgment from assessment data. Did the curriculum or tool work?
Evaluation is about the design's effectiveness for the next cohort, not one student's grade alone.
